messages.subject: Hessians
parts:
Hi all, 

For a model I'm currently optimizing I get to the objective tolerance I need considerably faster using Newton than LBFGS/BFGS. This got me curious how Newton was actually getting the Hessian, and it seems from what I understand of the code it's some hybrid of autodiff and finite differences which is O(N^2) - is that correct? Also from the Stan math code it seems full autodiff for the Hessian would be O(N^3) in general, which is presumably why you're not using that by default? 

Thanks!

David.

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Hessians
parts:
Is this a very simple problem or might it be a tuning issue
with our L-BFGS?

Full autodiff for Hessians requires N passes, so
it's O(N*f(N)) where f(N) is the cost of the density eval,
which is usually just N, so it's usually O(N^2). It gets
worse if there are operations like matrix factorizations
involved, where it usually goes up to O(N^2.5).

The reason we haven't used autodiff everywhere for Hessians
is lack of thorough testing, but we have everything at least basically
tested now, so we're going to be switching over to autodiff.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Hessians
parts:
Great. Am I right in thinking the Hessian calculation machinery is not currently directed exposed in rstan (as the gradient is in log_prob)? That would be nice to have. 

As for my model(s), I think it's a problem that may be somewhat specific to my setting: in general your LBFGS implementation seems to work great. I'm fitting two models, a null and alternative, and doing a likelihood ratio test, so I care a lot about the accuracy of the two likelihoods at convergence. I set all the tolerance options to optimizing to 0 apart from tol_obj, and I suspect at the optimum the likelihood surface is pretty flat wrt to some of the parameters (specifically those controlling count overdispersion). These are typically pretty small models (e.g. N=10), so not too surprising that Newton is competitive. I'm running a million or so of them (it's a genomics application) so I still care about runtime (which to be clear isn't bad already, just could be better). Maybe I should initialize Newton with LBFGS...
